summary: This informational RFC makes specifications of cryptographic algorithms based on the Russian national standards GOST R 34.10-2012 and GOST R 34.11-2012 available to the Internet community. They cover pseudorandom functions, key agreement based on Diffie-Hellman, and a hash function for use in cryptographic protocols.

eli5.summary: A recipe book for secret-code tools from Russian national standards, shared so other programmers can build them into Internet software.

subtitle: Russian cryptographic standards for protocols and key management

tldr.problem: International protocols need access to Russian cryptographic standards GOST R 34.10-2012 and GOST R 34.11-2012 to ensure interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides detailed specifications for HMAC functions, pseudorandom functions, key agreement (VKO), key derivation (KDF), and key wrapping based on these Russian standards.
tldr.outcome: Developers worldwide can now implement compatible versions of these algorithms for use in TLS, IKEv2, and other security protocols.

today: RFC 7836 is an Informational RFC published by the Independent Submission stream. It remains current as the standard reference for implementing GOST R 34.10-2012 and GOST R 34.11-2012 based protocols on the Internet.

sections.title: Introduction to GOST Algorithms
sections.content:
RFC 7836 documents cryptographic algorithms based on Russian national standards, GOST R 34.10-2012 (for digital signatures) and GOST R 34.11-2012 (for hashing). This RFC makes these specifications available in English so the Internet community can implement compatible versions for use in cryptographic protocols.

The RFC describes the pseudorandom functions, key agreement algorithms based on the Diffie-Hellman method, hash functions, key derivation functions, and key wrapping mechanisms that are necessary for protocols like TLS and IKEv2 to work across systems using Russian standards.
sections.eli5: This document is a guide to Russian secret-code rules, translated so Internet programmers anywhere can use them.

sections.title: HMAC and Pseudorandom Functions
sections.content:
The RFC defines HMAC (Hashed-based Message Authentication Code) transformations using the GOST R 34.11-2012 hash function. Two variants are specified: HMAC_GOSTR3411_2012_256 produces 32-byte output, and HMAC_GOSTR3411_2012_512 produces 64-byte output.

For TLS protocol use, the RFC defines PRF_TLS_GOSTR3411_2012_256 and PRF_TLS_GOSTR3411_2012_512, which use these HMAC functions to generate pseudorandom sequences. For IKEv2 protocol, the HMAC functions can directly serve as PRF functions, supporting both 256-bit and 512-bit key generation.
sections.eli5: Think of HMAC as a special signature that proves a message came from someone with the right secret key. This RFC gives recipes for two different strength levels.

sections.title: Key Agreement and Derivation
sections.content:
The RFC specifies two VKO (key agreement) algorithms based on GOST R 34.10-2012. VKO_GOSTR3410_2012_256 produces 256-bit keys and works with public keys of 512 bits or larger. VKO_GOSTR3410_2012_512 produces 512-bit keys and requires public keys of 1024 bits or larger. Both use elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman and take an optional User Keying Material (UKM) parameter.

Two key derivation functions (KDF) are defined. KDF_TREE_GOSTR3411_2012_256 is a tree-based function that can generate keying material of variable size, supporting hierarchical key management. KDF_GOSTR3411_2012_256 is a simpler single-level variant that generates 256-bit keys.
sections.eli5: When two parties want to agree on a secret key over a public channel, these functions do the math. The tree version lets you build a whole hierarchy of keys from one master key.

sections.title: Elliptic Curve Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC provides parameter sets for elliptic curves in two forms. The canonical form (short Weierstrass form) is defined by the equation y^2 = x^3 + ax + b (mod p). Two 512-bit parameter sets are specified: paramSetA and paramSetB, while 256-bit curves use parameters from RFC 4357.

The twisted Edwards form provides alternative representations with equivalent security. Parameter sets are given for 256-bit and 512-bit curves, with coordinate transformation formulas allowing conversion between canonical and Edwards forms. Each parameter set has a unique object identifier for use in protocols.
sections.eli5: An elliptic curve is a special mathematical shape used to protect secrets. This RFC lists the exact shapes and numbers to use, with two different ways of describing the same curves.

sections.title: Key Wrap and Protection
sections.content:
The RFC specifies how to encrypt and protect keys using GOST 28147-89 encryption with key derivation for export. The wrapping process generates a random seed, derives an encryption key from the export key using KDF_GOSTR3411_2012_256, calculates a 4-byte MAC for integrity, and encrypts the key in ECB mode.

The wrapped key consists of the seed, the encrypted key material, and the MAC. To unwrap, the same steps are reversed: the encryption key is derived again, the key is decrypted, and the MAC is verified. This ensures that wrapped keys cannot be tampered with during transport or storage.
sections.eli5: Imagine putting a secret key in a locked box before sending it: you add a protective cover with a seal to prove nobody opened it. Unwrapping checks that the seal is still good before trusting the key.
